title: X Feed Digest
page_title: X Feed Digest — Saturday, April 11th, 2026 — 9:00 AM ET
summary: Agent tooling—not raw model hype—dominated the batch: OpenAI repriced Codex-heavy usage, Codex itself shipped a meaningful runtime update, and Anthropic kept moving agent infrastructure deeper into the platform.

Memory and context management look increasingly like the real leverage point for useful agents, with GBrain pushing a full personal-memory stack while smaller tools focused on shrinking token waste from noisy command output.

The strongest AI adoption signal was organizational rather than technical: the best thread argued companies win by making AI usage socially normal and expected, not by forcing top-down training theater.

Macro discussion leaned toward tighter-money realism. Bank earnings start next week, Jamie Dimon’s “cheap money is over” thesis is still echoing through the feed, and Japan’s housing-market dysfunction got reframed as tax distortion rather than hidden bargain inventory.

Outside pure AI and markets, the most useful posts were operator-level: better remote setups for supervising agents, a clear founder-era timeline for the last six years of startup whiplash, and a reminder that privacy abuses can still unwind years later in court.

items.title: @OpenAI: New $100 Codex-Focused Tier
items.body: OpenAI said it is adding a new $100/month Pro tier with materially more Codex usage than Plus, while keeping the $200 plan as the highest-usage option and extending a temporary 2x Codex promo for existing top-tier users. The real signal is that heavy coding-agent demand is now strong enough to force explicit product segmentation instead of one-size-fits-all subscriptions.

items.title: @Codex_Changelog: Codex 0.120.0 Improves Agent Ops
items.body: Codex 0.120.0 adds live progress streaming for running agents, cleaner separation between live and completed hooks in the TUI, thread titles in custom status lines, and typed outputSchema support for MCP tools. It is a practical release rather than a flashy one, but exactly the kind of runtime polish that makes agent sessions easier to supervise and integrate.

items.title: @dotey: Anthropic Managed Agents Get Safer Credential Handling
items.body: A strong explainer on Anthropic’s new Vaults model said per-user credentials can be injected for agent tool use without ever appearing inside the model context window. That matters because it is the right architectural answer to prompt-injection risk: the model can use secrets without being able to casually read or leak them.

items.title: @garrytan: GBrain Open-Sources a Personal Memory Stack
items.body: Garry Tan open-sourced the markdown-heavy memory system behind his own agent workflow, built to recall thousands of notes, people files, meetings, and calendar entries. The broader takeaway is that production-grade agent usefulness is being won through memory architecture and retrieval discipline, not just better base models.

items.title: @AYi_AInotes: Ramp’s AI Adoption Playbook Is Mostly Culture
items.body: The best enterprise-AI thread in the batch argued that Ramp drove adoption by making AI use visible, expected, and socially reinforced across the company rather than burying employees in mandatory training. If true, that is a useful correction for teams still treating AI rollout as a procurement problem instead of a behavior-design problem.

items.title: @GitHub_Daily: RTK Cuts Context Waste for Coding Agents
items.body: One practical tool recommendation highlighted RTK, which filters and compresses noisy terminal output before it gets stuffed into Claude Code, Codex, or similar workflows. The pitch is simple but credible: if your agent keeps burning tokens on repetitive git status and test logs, better output shaping may buy more value than switching models again.

items.title: @FactSet: Bank Earnings Start Next Week
items.body: FactSet’s preview laid out a dense bank-earnings calendar starting April 13, with big U.S. names reporting through midweek and analysts looking for better year-over-year results on loan growth and asset repricing. For anyone watching macro tone, this is one of the next clean checkpoints for how much higher-rate pressure is still helping versus hurting the sector.

items.title: @RockportAI: Dimon’s “Cheap Money Is Over” View Is Spreading
items.body: A digest of Jamie Dimon’s latest letter pushed the idea that the era of easy money is not just paused but structurally gone. Even secondhand, it is a useful framing device for markets: if that regime view is right, investors should be slower to assume old valuation shortcuts and fast rebounds will keep working.

items.title: @aakashgupta: Japan’s Empty Homes Are a Tax Story, Not a Value Story
items.body: Aakash Gupta’s thread argued that Japan’s millions of abandoned homes are largely the product of tax incentives that punish demolition and reward leaving decaying structures standing, rather than evidence of some giant overlooked real-estate bargain. That is a sharp, useful reminder that market weirdness often comes from policy plumbing before it comes from investor neglect.

items.title: @mronge: Headless Mac mini + iPad Is a Strong Agent Console
items.body: A short demo made the case for using a headless Mac mini as the always-on agent box and an iPad as the mobile control surface for monitoring, taking over, and steering work remotely. It is a niche setup, but a very sensible one if your agents increasingly live in long-running terminal sessions.

items.title: @ChrisJBakke: The Last Six Years Were a Founder Stress Test
items.body: Chris Bakke compressed the startup environment from 2020 through 2026 into one brutal sequence of regime shifts: pandemic chaos, easy-money excess, talent inflation, bank instability, and then the AI/crypto/defense narrative carousel. It landed because it explains why many operators feel exhausted even when execution has been decent.

items.title: @NCLAlegal: Massachusetts Settles Over Silent Covid Tracking App Install
items.body: One of the more consequential non-AI posts surfaced a settlement over a Massachusetts program that allegedly auto-installed a Covid tracking app on more than a million phones without meaningful consent. It is a useful reminder that privacy violations disguised as public-interest tech can take years to unwind, but they do not disappear just because the news cycle moved on.
